prompt: The only intentional difference between Experiments 1 and 2 was:

choices.text: The volume of acid in the flask was varied in Experiment 2 but held constant in Experiment 1
choices.rationale: The volume of acid in the flask was kept the same in both experiments; only the concentration of the base changed.

choices.text: The concentration of the acid was held constant in Experiment 2 but varied in Experiment 1
choices.rationale: Both experiments tested the same set of values of acid concentration.

choices.text: A different quantity was measured in Experiment 2 in place of the volume of base needed
choices.rationale: Both experiments measured the volume of base needed.

choices.text: The concentration of the base was 0.10 M base in Experiment 1 and 0.20 M base in Experiment 2
choices.rationale: Correct. The description of Experiment 2 says the procedure was repeated with only this condition changed.

explanation: Experiment 2 repeated Experiment 1 using a 0.20 M base solution; everything else, including the values of acid concentration and the quantity measured, stayed the same.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students placed 25 mL of an acid solution of known concentration in a flask with a few drops of indicator using a 0.10 M base solution and added base solution from a burette, swirling, until the indicator changed color. They recorded the volume of base added. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated using a 0.20 M base solution, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: Which of the following hypotheses is best supported by the results of Experiment 1?

choices.text: The volume of acid in the flask determines base volume.
choices.rationale: The volume of acid in the flask was held constant, so the experiment says nothing about its effect.

choices.text: Increasing acid concentration increases base volume.
choices.rationale: Correct. Every increase in the independent variable produced a larger measured value.

choices.text: Acid concentration has no effect on base volume.
choices.rationale: The measured values change clearly from trial to trial, so there is an effect.

choices.text: Increasing acid concentration decreases base volume.
choices.rationale: The results do not fall with every increase in the independent variable.

explanation: Reading the results in order of acid concentration, the volume of base needed increased, which supports: "Increasing acid concentration increases base volume."

stimulus.title: Acid Concentration and Titration
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students placed 25 mL of an acid solution of known concentration in a flask with a few drops of indicator and added base solution from a burette, swirling, until the indicator changed color. They recorded the volume of base added.
Results (the volume of base needed): at 0.05 mol/L, 8.6 mL; at 0.1 mol/L, 17.3 mL; at 0.15 mol/L, 25.9 mL; at 0.2 mol/L, 34.6 mL; at 0.25 mol/L, 43.2 mL.

prompt: In Experiment 1, the experimenters repeated each measurement several times and recorded the average. The most likely reason was to:

choices.text: Make the horizontal distance the ball traveled change more in response to launch angle
choices.rationale: Repeating a measurement cannot change the size of the real effect.

choices.text: Remove the need to keep the compression of the spring the same
choices.rationale: Repetition does not substitute for controlling variables; controls are still needed.

choices.text: Reduce the effect of random error in individual measurements
choices.rationale: Correct. Averaging repeated measurements cancels out much of the random variation in any single measurement.

choices.text: Increase the range of launch angle that could be tested
choices.rationale: Repeating a measurement does not change which values of launch angle are tested.

explanation: Any single measurement contains random error; repeating and averaging makes the recorded value more reliable.

stimulus.title: Launch Angle and Range
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students used a spring launcher to fire the same ball at a set angle above the horizontal, always with the spring compressed by the same amount. They measured the horizontal distance from the launcher to the landing point. Each angle was fired three times and the average distance recorded.
Results (the horizontal distance the ball traveled): at 20°, 21.4 m; at 30°, 27.5 m; at 40°, 29.8 m; at 50°, 28.6 m; at 60°, 24.2 m; at 70°, 17.5 m.

prompt: If Experiment 1 were extended with a trial at 55 mm, the flow rate of the river would most likely have been:

choices.text: between 31.5 m³/s and 40.1 m³/s
choices.rationale: Correct. 55 mm is between the tested values 50 mm and 60 mm, whose results were 31.5 and 40.1.

choices.text: between 23.9 m³/s and 31.5 m³/s
choices.rationale: This interval belongs to rainfall between 40 mm and 50 mm.

choices.text: below every result obtained, less than 12.1 m³/s
choices.rationale: This is below every result; the trend gives no reason to expect it.

choices.text: above every result obtained, greater than 40.1 m³/s
choices.rationale: This is above every result; the trend gives no reason to expect it.

explanation: The results change steadily with rainfall, so a trial at 55 mm should give a value between those of its neighbors, 31.5 and 40.1 m³/s.

stimulus.title: Rainfall and River Flow
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Hydrologists measured the flow rate of a river at a gauging station the morning after rainfall events of several sizes. Rainfall was recorded at a weather station in the river's drainage basin.
Results (the flow rate of the river): at 20 mm, 12.1 m³/s; at 30 mm, 17.4 m³/s; at 40 mm, 23.9 m³/s; at 50 mm, 31.5 m³/s; at 60 mm, 40.1 m³/s.

prompt: The experimenters tested 6 different values of the thickness of the insulation rather than just two. The most likely reason was to:

choices.text: Make each individual measurement of the rate of heat loss more precise than it would otherwise be
choices.rationale: The precision of a single measurement depends on the instrument and repetition, not on how many values of the independent variable are tested.

choices.text: Remove the need to hold the room temperature constant during the trials
choices.rationale: Testing more values does not replace controlling other variables.

choices.text: Keep the rate of heat loss the same from one trial to the next so that the trials could be compared
choices.rationale: The dependent variable is measured, not held constant; it is expected to change.

choices.text: Show how the rate of heat loss changes across the whole range, not just at its two ends
choices.rationale: Correct. Two points can only show a difference; several points show the shape of the relationship.

explanation: Measuring at several values of insulation thickness lets the experimenters see the pattern of the relationship, not just whether the two ends differ.

stimulus.title: Insulation and Heat Loss
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students wrapped a metal box containing an electric heater in foam sheets of a set total thickness. They adjusted the heater power until the inside temperature held steady in a 20°C room and recorded that power as the rate of heat loss.
Results (the rate of heat loss): at 0 cm, 156 W; at 2 cm, 91 W; at 4 cm, 64 W; at 6 cm, 50 W; at 8 cm, 41 W; at 10 cm, 34 W.

prompt: If the experimenters wanted their measurements of the activity of the enzyme to be more reliable, they should most likely:

choices.text: Test fewer values of pH so that each individual trial can be done more quickly
choices.rationale: Fewer values give less information and do nothing to reduce random error.

choices.text: Record the activity of the enzyme to fewer decimal places to simplify the table
choices.rationale: Rounding discards information; it cannot make the results more trustworthy.

choices.text: Allow the volume of enzyme solution to vary freely from one trial to the next
choices.rationale: Letting a controlled variable vary adds a confounding factor and makes results less reliable.

choices.text: Repeat each trial several more times at each pH and average the results
choices.rationale: Correct. Averaging more repeated trials reduces the effect of random error.

explanation: Reliability improves when random variation is averaged out by more repetitions or larger samples, while everything else is held constant.

stimulus.title: Enzyme Activity and pH
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students added 1 mL of enzyme solution to tubes containing a substrate solution buffered to a set pH. They measured how much product formed in 5 minutes to find the activity. Each pH was tested in triplicate.
Results (the activity of the enzyme): at pH 3, 4 µmol/min; at pH 4, 19 µmol/min; at pH 5, 44 µmol/min; at pH 6, 51 µmol/min; at pH 7, 29 µmol/min; at pH 8, 8 µmol/min.

prompt: The only intentional difference between Experiments 1 and 2 was:

choices.text: The earthquake recorded was Quake 1 in Experiment 1 and Quake 2 in Experiment 2
choices.rationale: Correct. The description of Experiment 2 says the procedure was repeated with only this condition changed.

choices.text: A different quantity was measured in Experiment 2 in place of the maximum ground motion
choices.rationale: Both experiments measured the maximum ground motion.

choices.text: The distance from the epicenter was held constant in Experiment 2 but varied in Experiment 1
choices.rationale: Both experiments tested the same set of values of distance.

choices.text: The type of seismograph was varied in Experiment 2 but held constant in Experiment 1
choices.rationale: The type of seismograph was kept the same in both experiments; only the earthquake recorded changed.

explanation: Experiment 2 repeated Experiment 1 for Quake 2, a larger earthquake at the same location; everything else, including the values of distance and the quantity measured, stayed the same.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Seismologists compared the maximum ground motion recorded by identical seismographs at several distances from the epicenter of an earthquake for Quake 1. All stations stood on the same type of bedrock. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated for Quake 2, a larger earthquake at the same location, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: Based on Experiment 1, which conclusion is best supported?

choices.text: Increasing time increases voltage.
choices.rationale: The results do not rise with every increase in the independent variable.

choices.text: The lamp used determines voltage.
choices.rationale: The lamp used was held constant, so the experiment says nothing about its effect.

choices.text: Time has no effect on voltage.
choices.rationale: The measured values change clearly from trial to trial, so there is an effect.

choices.text: Increasing time decreases voltage.
choices.rationale: Correct. Every increase in the independent variable produced a smaller measured value.

explanation: Reading the results in order of time, the voltage of the battery decreased, which supports: "Increasing time decreases voltage."

stimulus.title: Battery Voltage Over Time
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students connected a fresh AA battery to a small lamp and measured the battery's voltage with a voltmeter at regular intervals while the lamp stayed on.
Results (the voltage of the battery): at 2 h, 1.48 V; at 4 h, 1.40 V; at 6 h, 1.29 V; at 8 h, 1.16 V; at 10 h, 1.00 V.

prompt: Why did the experimenters most likely repeat each measurement several times and record the average in Experiment 1?

choices.text: Reduce the effect of random error in individual measurements
choices.rationale: Correct. Averaging repeated measurements cancels out much of the random variation in any single measurement.

choices.text: Make the rate of photosynthesis change more in response to light intensity
choices.rationale: Repeating a measurement cannot change the size of the real effect.

choices.text: Remove the need to keep the temperature of the water the same
choices.rationale: Repetition does not substitute for controlling variables; controls are still needed.

choices.text: Increase the range of light intensity that could be tested
choices.rationale: Repeating a measurement does not change which values of light intensity are tested.

explanation: Any single measurement contains random error; repeating and averaging makes the recorded value more reliable.

stimulus.title: Light and Photosynthesis
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students placed a sprig of pondweed in a test tube of water and set a lamp at distances giving several light intensities. They counted the oxygen bubbles released in one minute at each intensity, repeating each count three times.
Results (the rate of photosynthesis): at 200 µmol/m²/s, 19.4 bubbles/min; at 300 µmol/m²/s, 21.5 bubbles/min; at 400 µmol/m²/s, 22.7 bubbles/min; at 500 µmol/m²/s, 23.6 bubbles/min; at 600 µmol/m²/s, 24.1 bubbles/min.

prompt: Suppose the experimenters had run one more trial in Experiment 1 at an altitude of 1750 m. Based on the results, the boiling point of the water in that trial would most likely have been:

choices.text: above every result obtained, greater than 100.0 °C
choices.rationale: This is above every result; the trend gives no reason to expect it.

choices.text: below every result obtained, less than 92.1 °C
choices.rationale: This is below every result; the trend gives no reason to expect it.

choices.text: between 92.1 °C and 93.7 °C
choices.rationale: This interval belongs to altitude between 2000 m and 2500 m.

choices.text: between 93.7 °C and 95.3 °C
choices.rationale: Correct. 1750 m is between the tested values 1500 m and 2000 m, whose results were 93.7 and 95.3.

explanation: The results change steadily with altitude, so a trial at 1750 m should give a value between those of its neighbors, 93.7 and 95.3 °C.

stimulus.title: Altitude and Boiling Point
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
A team carried the same kettle, thermometer, and a measured volume of distilled water to stations at several altitudes. At each station the water was heated until it boiled steadily and the temperature was recorded.
Results (the boiling point of the water): at 0 m, 100.0 °C; at 500 m, 98.4 °C; at 1000 m, 96.8 °C; at 1500 m, 95.3 °C; at 2000 m, 93.7 °C; at 2500 m, 92.1 °C.

prompt: The experimenters tested 5 different values of the speed of the car rather than just two. The most likely reason was to:

choices.text: Remove the need to hold the car and its tires constant during the trials
choices.rationale: Testing more values does not replace controlling other variables.

choices.text: Make each individual measurement of the stopping distance more precise than it would otherwise be
choices.rationale: The precision of a single measurement depends on the instrument and repetition, not on how many values of the independent variable are tested.

choices.text: Keep the stopping distance the same from one trial to the next so that the trials could be compared
choices.rationale: The dependent variable is measured, not held constant; it is expected to change.

choices.text: Show how the stopping distance changes across the whole range, not just at its two ends
choices.rationale: Correct. Two points can only show a difference; several points show the shape of the relationship.

explanation: Measuring at several values of speed lets the experimenters see the pattern of the relationship, not just whether the two ends differ.

stimulus.title: Speed and Stopping Distance
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
On a closed test track, a driver brought the same car to each test speed, then braked as hard as possible when a signal light flashed. The distance from the signal to the stopping point was measured. Each speed was tested three times and the average distance recorded.
Results (the stopping distance): at 40 km/h, 18.5 m; at 60 km/h, 34.7 m; at 80 km/h, 55.7 m; at 100 km/h, 81.4 m; at 120 km/h, 111.8 m.

prompt: Which of the following changes to Experiment 1 would most improve the reliability of its results?

choices.text: Record the maximum ground motion to fewer decimal places to simplify the table
choices.rationale: Rounding discards information; it cannot make the results more trustworthy.

choices.text: Allow the type of seismograph to vary freely from one trial to the next
choices.rationale: Letting a controlled variable vary adds a confounding factor and makes results less reliable.

choices.text: Repeat each trial several more times at each distance and average the results
choices.rationale: Correct. Averaging more repeated trials reduces the effect of random error.

choices.text: Test fewer values of distance so that each individual trial can be done more quickly
choices.rationale: Fewer values give less information and do nothing to reduce random error.

explanation: Reliability improves when random variation is averaged out by more repetitions or larger samples, while everything else is held constant.

stimulus.title: Earthquake Distance and Shaking
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Seismologists compared the maximum ground motion recorded by identical seismographs at several distances from the epicenter of an earthquake. All stations stood on the same type of bedrock.
Results (the maximum ground motion): at 50 km, 4.32 mm; at 100 km, 1.53 mm; at 150 km, 0.83 mm; at 200 km, 0.54 mm; at 250 km, 0.39 mm; at 300 km, 0.29 mm.
